subject: mathematics
question_text: Using the principle of finite Mathematical Induction, prove that a + ar + ar² + … upto n terms = a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1), for r ≠ 1.

mark_split.label: Write the nth term and the statement

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Junior Inter Maths-1A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.99 — from the book's separate "STAR QUESTIONS PLUS" bank, answer 144. That bank (book pp.98-111, answers 142-180) sits AFTER all the numbered chapters and is organised by chapter rather than forming part of any chapter's inventory; it is authored into this unit because that is where the question belongs on the paper (founder decision 2026-08-22). SECTION: the bank gives no mark cut here, but Mathematical Induction is an LAQ-ONLY unit — the paper gives it only Q19 — so the section is fixed by the unit, not inferred. Printed appearances: AP 19 · TS 20. The geometric-progression sum, proved by induction. It uses the SAME five moves as every answer in Unit 2 — nth term, S(1), assume S(k), prove S(k+1), conclude by P.M.I. ⚠ THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S — the bank prints no [N Marks] tags anywhere. The shapes used follow the splits the book DOES print elsewhere: 1+1 for a 2-mark VSAQ (answers 100, 101 on book p.82), 1+1+1+1 or 1+2+1 for a 4-mark SAQ (answers 58, 59 on p.63 and 61 on p.64), and the granular 1x7 for a 7-mark LAQ (answer 32 on p.44). recall_prompt: Say how you would do this one — name each move in order.

steps.label: Write the nth term and the statement
steps.margin_note: First mark. The nth term of the series is arⁿ⁻¹ — note the n−1, since the first term has no r at all.
lines: Let S(n): a + ar + … + arⁿ⁻¹ = a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1)

recall.must_convey: That the nth term is arⁿ⁻¹ and the statement S(n) is written out.
accept: the nth term is a r to the n minus one and write the statement S of n
note that the first term has no r so the power is n minus one
state what has to be proved as S of n
nth term a r power n minus one, S of n rasta
write the nth term and the statement
heard_as: a r to the n minus one

steps.why: The power is n−1 because the series starts at r⁰. Getting that wrong shifts every later step by one term.
common_mistakes: Writing the nth term as arⁿ.

steps.label: Verify S(1)
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Put n = 1 into both sides. The right side needs the (r−1) to cancel, which it does exactly.

recall.must_convey: That n = 1 gives a on both sides, so S(1) is true.
accept: put n equals one, the left is a and the right is a r minus one over r minus one which is a
both sides come to a so S one holds
the r minus one cancels leaving a
n equals one pettithe rendu vaipula a vasthundi
verify the base case

steps.why: r ≠ 1 is what makes the cancellation legal — with r = 1 the right side would be 0/0 and the formula would not exist at all.

steps.label: Assume S(k)
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Assume the statement holds for some k and write it down — this is the induction hypothesis, and the next step leans on it entirely.
lines: Assume S(k) is true for some k ∈ N:

recall.must_convey: That S(k) is assumed true and written out as an equation to be used later.
accept: assume S of k is true and write it out as equation one
take the statement as true for k
write the induction hypothesis
S of k true ani assume chesi rasta
assume it holds for some k

steps.why: The hypothesis is the only thing the next step is allowed to use. Writing it as a numbered equation is what makes the substitution visible.
common_mistakes: Assuming what has to be proved.

steps.label: Prove S(k+1)
steps.margin_note: Three marks — the bulk. Add the (k+1)th term, which is ar^k, to both sides of the hypothesis, then combine over the common denominator.
lines: Adding the (k+1)th term ar^k to both sides of (1):

recall.must_convey: That ar^k is added to both sides, combined over (r−1), and the ar^k terms cancel to give a(r^(k+1) − 1)/(r − 1).
accept: add a r to the k to both sides then combine over r minus one and the a r to the k terms cancel
the two middle terms cancel leaving a r to the k plus one minus a
it becomes the statement with k plus one in place of k
a r power k add chesi combine cheste cancel avthai
prove the k plus one case

steps.why: +ar^k and −ar^k cancel exactly, which is the whole reason the formula closes. If they did not, the induction would fail.
common_mistakes: Not putting the two terms over a common denominator.

steps.label: Conclude by P.M.I.
steps.margin_note: Last mark. Both halves are done, so the principle applies. Name it — that sentence is the mark.
lines: S(1) is true, and S(k) true ⇒ S(k+1) true.

lines.text: ∴ By P.M.I., S(n) is true for all n ∈ N.

recall.must_convey: That both the base case and the inductive step hold, so by the principle of mathematical induction S(n) is true for all n.
accept: S one is true and S k implies S k plus one so by the principle it holds for all n
invoke the principle of mathematical induction
both parts done so it is true for every n
P M I prakaram anni n ki true
conclude by induction

steps.why: Induction needs both halves and the sentence that joins them. Stopping after S(k+1) leaves the proof formally unfinished.
common_mistakes: Writing "hence proved" without naming the principle.
